title: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins
subtitle: A ninja succeeds by remaining unseen

body: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins is Acquire's PlayStation stealth game, first released in Japan on 26 February 1998. Rikimaru and Ayame undertake missions for Lord Gohda in a fictionalised Sengoku-era Japan. The player chooses a ninja, prepares equipment and enters a place where observing guards matters more than winning a public fight. Rooftops and concealed approaches provide room to plan. The game makes the ninja's familiar tools into practical ways of moving through three-dimensional space, asking the player to arrange an encounter before the enemy knows that an encounter has begun.

The grappling hook gives access to high positions from which patrols and possible routes can be studied. Other tools can distract, delay or harm a guard, but only a limited selection can be carried into a mission. Rikimaru and Ayame differ in speed and fighting style, changing how an exposed situation feels. Remaining unseen creates opportunities for quiet attacks; being discovered forces a less comfortable response. Each successful approach begins with reading the space, then choosing when to move from safety into the guard's reach.

Acquire began production in 1996 with a small team, and director Takuma Endo took on several roles, including scenario writing. Noriyuki Asakura's music supported a setting unusual among the period's modern military stealth games. Activision published the Western editions later in 1998, bringing the game to a wider audience. Its reception and sales led to Tenchu 2 in 2000. The original's lasting image is an ordinary stretch of roof above an unsuspecting guard: a simple arrangement that gives the player time to watch, choose and act.
